title: ECHO-7 Case Database
notice: Curated research starter set. Not a live feed. Sources and summaries should be reviewed before publication; unresolved reports are not evidence of extraterrestrial origin.

cases.title: USS Nimitz / “Tic Tac”
cases.label: Military report
cases.summary: Navy aviators reported unusual objects during training operations in November 2004. The event became widely discussed after public reporting and release of Navy video.
cases.question: What can the available video, testimony, and sensor records establish about the observed object?
cases.evidence: A public video and pilot accounts do not, by themselves, establish an object's origin or technology.
cases.status: Publicly documented; full underlying sensor record is not all publicly available.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Defense video statement

cases.title: Phoenix Lights
cases.label: Mass sighting
cases.summary: Witnesses reported lights and formations over Arizona on March 13, 1997. Different observations may have involved different events and should not automatically be treated as one object or explanation.
cases.question: Which observations can be connected to specific times, locations, and explanations?
cases.evidence: Eyewitness reports are useful records, but distance, perspective, and timing affect interpretation.

cases.title: Roswell Incident
cases.label: Historic controversy
cases.summary: Reports of recovered debris near Roswell became central to modern UFO folklore. Later U.S. Air Force reports connected the material to a classified balloon project; some witnesses and researchers dispute aspects of the official account.
cases.question: What do contemporaneous records show, and which claims rely on later testimony?
cases.evidence: Controversy is not itself proof of an extraterrestrial crash. Compare primary records with later recollections.
cases.status: Official explanations and alternative claims remain subjects of public debate.

sources.label: U.S. Air Force report archive (via National Archives)

cases.title: GIMBAL
cases.label: Military video
cases.summary: GIMBAL is among the Navy videos publicly released by the Department of Defense. Interpreting apparent motion requires attention to camera behavior, viewing geometry, and limits of the recording.
cases.question: Which apparent movements belong to the object, and which could be caused by the sensor?
cases.evidence: The video documents an observation, but the clip alone does not conclusively identify the object.
cases.status: Public video; not a complete public sensor dataset.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Defense video statement

cases.title: Project Blue Book
cases.label: Government investigation
cases.summary: The U.S. Air Force's Project Blue Book collected and assessed UFO reports. Its files are a historical record of reports and investigations, not a general finding that the cases were extraterrestrial.
cases.question: How were reports categorized, and what can the archive tell us about the limits of historical investigations?
cases.evidence: A case marked unidentified means the available information did not resolve it under that investigation; it does not establish a specific origin.
cases.status: Historical program; records are available through the U.S. National Archives.

cases.title: Modern UAP reporting framework
cases.label: Research framework
cases.summary: NASA and the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office publish research and reporting materials intended to improve data quality, analysis, and public understanding of UAP.
cases.question: What data would be needed to distinguish an ordinary object, sensor artifact, or genuinely unresolved observation?
cases.evidence: Unidentified is a status of analysis, not a conclusion about extraterrestrial origin.

cases.title: The search for life beyond Earth
cases.label: Astrobiology
cases.summary: Scientists investigate habitability and possible biosignatures using planetary missions, laboratory research, and observations of planets beyond our Solar System. No confirmed discovery of extraterrestrial life has been announced by NASA.
cases.question: What would count as convincing evidence of life, and how would scientists rule out non-biological explanations?
cases.evidence: Habitability is not the same as evidence that life exists; a potential biosignature requires independent validation.
cases.status: Active scientific research; no confirmed extraterrestrial life detection.
